exons are demarcated in the three-dimensional structure and that they colocalize with regulatory elements, such as promoters and enhancers.
exons that exhibit a DNase I–hypersenstitivity signal colocalize with the promoters and distal enhancers that regulate their transcription.

DNase I-hypersensitive exons are associated with promoters and distals regulatory elements and that the association is enriched for alternative spicing events, an effect that is reflected in the cell type-specific peri-exonic DNase I-hyersensitive patterns.

how the three-dimensional organization of the genome influences transcriptional regulation.
the role of chromatin structure in the regulation of gene expression.
the role that chromatin structure plays in gene expression.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the DNase hypersensitive sites in the human genome are associated with promoters and enhancer elements.
the DNase I hypersensitive sites in exons are a consequence of the interaction of exons with enhancer and promoters, which are the main regulators of gene expression.
exons, promoters and enhancers interact with each other to form a functional unit, which is essential for the regulation of alternative splicing.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the three-dimensional genome structure of human cells is reflected in ChIP-seq, which is particularly evident at DNase I-hypersensitive exons.
the genome is folded in a way that allows for the capture of regulatory signals in chromatin and that this folding is important for the splicing process.
the genome is a three-dimensional structure and this structure is related to gene expression.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DNase I hypersensitive sites (DHSs) are not only associated with transcription factor binding, but also with the splicing of exons.
the genome is organized to allow for the efficient cotranscriptional capture of exons by promoters and enhancers.
exons, in addition to being the functional units that encode protein domains, are also structural components that contribute to the three-dimensional organization of the genome.
